1What You Will Learn

  • Place a system in the right risk class and say what each class means
  • List the requirements for high-risk systems and the duties that come with them
  • Explain human oversight, transparency and quality management
  • Explain the extra rules for general-purpose AI models
  • Explain enforcement and penalties, and how duties differ by role
  • Compare the South Korean, US and other approaches

2II.C.1: Explain the risk-classification scheme of AI laws and what falls in each class

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Understand, so the depth is Understand. The course has 2 practice questions on this indicator.

Running case

Which Helios System Is Regulated, and How?

  • The hiring tool screens EU applicants; Veridex also offers emotion analysis of the video interview
  • The customer assistant chats with EU customers on a Corvid Labs general-purpose model
  • Helios also hires in New York City, Illinois and Colorado and serves customers in South Korea
  • Jonas Weber asks: which class, which duties, which role, and what is the penalty if we get it wrong?

The EU AI Act at a Glance: Reach and Scope Beyond the BoK

  • The AI Act is the EU's risk-based regulation: the higher the risk, the heavier the duty
  • It applies to providers that place systems or general-purpose models on the EU market wherever they are based (Article 2)
  • And to deployers in the EU, and to third-country providers and deployers when the output is used in the EU
  • Also importers, distributors, product manufacturers, authorized representatives and affected persons in the EU
  • Excluded: military, defense and national security; research before market placement; purely personal non-professional use; certain open-source systems

Exam tip

Location of the provider does not matter; use in the EU does.

Key Definitions That Decide Scope Beyond the BoK

Term (Article 3) Why it matters
AI system (1) the machine-based system that infers outputs (module 1)
Provider (3) / Deployer (4) who develops and places on the market, and who uses under its authority
Placing on the market (9) the first making available on the Union market
Putting into service (11) supply for first use to the deployer, or for own use
General-purpose AI model (63) a model with significant generality, integrable in many systems
  • Intended purpose (set by the provider) drives classification: the same model can be minimal risk in one use and high-risk in another
  • A substantial modification can trigger new assessment and can change the role (Article 25)
Exam tip

Classification follows the use, not the technology.

The Four Risk Classes

  • Unacceptable risk: practices that are banned (Article 5)
  • High risk: allowed, but under strict requirements; two routes, Annex I (product safety) and Annex III (listed uses)
  • Limited risk: transparency duties, such as telling people they talk to AI (Article 50)
  • Minimal risk: no specific duties; voluntary codes
  • General-purpose AI models have their own track of obligations

Exam tip

Name the class first; the duties follow from it.

Prohibited Practices [Dates]

  • Manipulation and exploiting vulnerabilities (age, disability, social or economic situation)
  • Social scoring; crime prediction based solely on profiling
  • Face databases from untargeted scraping (internet or closed-circuit television, CCTV)
  • Emotion inference at work and in education, except for medical or safety reasons
  • Sensitive biometric categorization; real-time remote biometric identification for law enforcement, with limits
  • New: non-consensual intimate imagery and child sexual abuse material, from 2 December 2026; the older bans since 2 February 2025

Exam tip

Emotion recognition is banned at work and school but allowed for medical or safety reasons; elsewhere it is high-risk.

High-Risk, Route One: Product Safety (Annex I)

  • Route 1 (Article 6(1)): the system is a safety component of a product, or a product itself, under Annex I harmonized legislation, and that product needs a third-party conformity assessment
  • Typical: machinery, medical devices, vehicles, toys and similar regulated products
  • Route 2 (Article 6(2)): the system's use is listed in Annex III
  • Both routes lead to the same requirements (Articles 9 to 15), with different assessment procedures

Exam tip

Product-safety AI (a medical device component) and listed-use AI (hiring) are both high-risk, by different doors.

High-Risk, Route Two: The Annex III Areas Beyond the BoK

  • Biometrics (remote identification, categorization, emotion recognition)
  • Critical infrastructure safety components
  • Education: admission, assessing learning, monitoring tests
  • Employment: recruitment and selection (screening, evaluating candidates) and decisions on promotion, termination, task allocation and monitoring
  • Essential services: public benefits, credit scoring, life and health insurance pricing, emergency triage
  • Law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control, justice and democratic processes

Exam tip

Hiring and credit-scoring systems are high-risk by listing; fraud detection is carved out of the credit item.

Is It High-Risk? The Article 6(3) Filter Beyond the BoK

  • Step 1: is the practice prohibited? Stop.
  • Step 2: is it a safety component of an Annex I product? High-risk.
  • Step 3: is the use listed in Annex III? High-risk.
  • Step 4 (Article 6(3)): not high-risk only if it poses no significant risk of harm and fits one of four cases
  • The four cases: a narrow procedural task, improving a completed human activity, detecting patterns without replacing human assessment, or a preparatory task
  • But a system that performs profiling of natural persons is always high-risk
  • A provider that decides a listed system is not high-risk must document the assessment and register it (Article 6(4))

Exam tip

Profiling people on an Annex III use cannot be argued out of high-risk.

Limited and Minimal Risk, and General-Purpose Models

  • Limited risk: systems that interact with people, generate synthetic content or infer emotions carry transparency duties (Article 50, slide 22)
  • Minimal risk: most AI, such as spam filters; no specific duties, only voluntary codes
  • General-purpose AI models are a separate track: obligations fall on the model provider (slides 24 to 26)
  • A general-purpose model placed in a high-risk use makes the system high-risk, with the system's provider carrying those duties
  • The same company can be minimal-risk in one product and high-risk in another
Exam tip

A chatbot is limited risk for transparency, and becomes high-risk only if its use is on a high-risk list.

Applying the Classes to Helios

Helios system Class Why
Hiring tool (screens and ranks applicants) High-risk Annex III employment: recruitment and selection; profiling, so no Article 6(3) escape
Emotion analysis of the video interview Prohibited in the EU workplace Article 5 bans inferring emotions at work, except medical or safety reasons
Customer assistant (chat) Limited risk transparency: tell customers it is AI (Article 50)
Corvid Labs model underneath General-purpose model its provider has its own duties; Helios is its deployer
  • Result: Helios switches off emotion analysis for EU use and prepares for high-risk duties for the hiring tool
Exam tip

Walk the path in order: prohibited, high-risk, transparency, minimal.

3II.C.2: Explain the core requirements: risk management, data governance, documentation, assessments, records

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Understand, so the depth is Understand. The course has 1 practice question on this indicator.

The High-Risk Requirements at a Glance

  • Article 9 risk management system
  • Article 10 data and data governance
  • Article 11 technical documentation
  • Article 12 record-keeping (logs)
  • Article 13 transparency and instructions for use
  • Article 14 human oversight
  • Article 15 accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity
  • The provider must meet them; the deployer relies on and supports them

Exam tip

Learn the seven by their job: manage risk, govern data, document, log, tell, oversee, secure.

Risk Management System (Article 9)

  • A continuous, iterative process planned and run through the whole life cycle
  • Identify and analyze known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety and fundamental rights
  • Estimate and evaluate them, including from foreseeable misuse and post-market data
  • Adopt targeted measures and judge residual risk acceptable: design it out first, then mitigate, then inform and train
  • Test against predefined metrics before market placement
  • Consider persons under 18 and other vulnerable groups
Exam tip

Risk management is a living process, not a one-time assessment before launch.

Data and Data Governance (Article 10) Beyond the BoK [Verify live]

  • Governance covers design choices, data origin and collection, preparation (annotation, cleaning), assumptions, availability and suitability
  • Examine possible biases that could harm health, safety or fundamental rights or lead to prohibited discrimination, and take measures to detect, prevent and mitigate them
  • Datasets should be relevant, sufficiently representative, free of errors as far as possible and complete
  • The Digital Omnibus added Article 4a: special-category data may be processed exceptionally for bias detection and correction, only where strictly necessary and under strict conditions (no other data suffice, strong security, no transfer, deletion afterwards, records)
  • As of 27 October 2026: this rule is new; check the consolidated text
Exam tip

Bias examination is a legal duty for high-risk data, and the exception for sensitive data is narrow and recorded.

Technical Documentation and Record-Keeping (Articles 11 and 12)

  • Technical documentation is drawn up before placing on the market, kept up to date, and shows compliance; it has the minimum elements of Annex IV
  • SMEs may use a simplified form
  • A post-market monitoring plan is part of that documentation (slide 20)
  • Logs: the system must automatically record events over its lifetime, to identify risk situations, to support post-market monitoring and to let deployers monitor operation
  • Remote biometric identification logs add time of use, database checked, matched input and the people who verified
Exam tip

Documentation is for authorities and assessors; logs are for tracing what the system did.

Transparency to Deployers and Accuracy, Robustness, Cybersecurity (Articles 13 and 15)

  • Instructions for use must state the provider's identity, the system's capabilities and limits, pre-determined changes, human oversight measures, resources and lifetime, and log collection (Article 13)
  • Accuracy: declare the levels and metrics in the instructions
  • Robustness: resilient to errors, faults and inconsistencies; reduce feedback loops where the system keeps learning
  • Cybersecurity: resist attempts to alter use or output, including data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples and confidentiality attacks
Exam tip

Transparency here means information for the deployer to use the system properly; notices to the public are in Article 50.

Conformity Assessment, Declaration, CE Marking and Registration

  • Conformity assessment (Article 43): for most Annex III uses, internal control by the provider; for biometrics, internal control or a notified body, depending on standards; Annex I products follow the sectoral procedure
  • The provider draws up the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47) and affixes the CE marking (Article 48)
  • The system is registered (Article 49) before use
  • A substantial modification needs a new assessment; changes pre-determined for a learning system are not substantial

Exam tip

Providers of listed-use high-risk systems mostly self-assess; a notified body is the exception.

Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (Article 27)

  • Who: deployers that are public bodies or private entities providing public services, and deployers of credit-scoring and life and health insurance systems (Annex III points 5(b) and 5(c)); not for critical infrastructure systems
  • When: before first use; update if elements change
  • Content: the process, period and frequency of use, groups affected, specific risks of harm, human oversight, and measures if risks materialize, including complaint mechanisms
  • Notify the market surveillance authority; cross-refer to a GDPR DPIA where one exists

Exam tip

A deployer's FRIA complements the provider's risk management; a DPIA can supply parts of it.

Post-Market Monitoring and Serious Incident Reporting (Articles 72 and 73)

  • Post-market monitoring (Article 72): a system proportionate to the technology and risks that collects and analyzes performance data over the system's lifetime; the plan belongs to the technical documentation
  • Serious incidents (Article 73): report immediately after a causal link is established, and in any event not later than 15 days after awareness
  • Not later than 2 days for a widespread infringement or the most serious disruptions; not later than 10 days after a death
  • Deployers tell the provider and the authorities when they suspect a risk or a serious incident (Article 26)

Exam tip

Remember the order of urgency: 2 days, 10 days, 15 days.

4II.C.3: Explain the duties for human oversight, for transparency and notices, and for a quality-management system

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Understand, so the depth is Understand. The course has 1 practice question on this indicator.

Human Oversight (Article 14)

  • The aim is to prevent or minimize risks to health, safety and fundamental rights, including from foreseeable misuse
  • Overseers must be able to: understand the system's capacities and limits; stay aware of automation bias; interpret output correctly; override or disregard output or decide not to use it; stop the system
  • For remote biometric identification, a result is acted on only after separate verification by two people
  • The provider designs the measures in; the deployer assigns competent, trained people with authority (Article 26)

Exam tip

Oversight must be effective: a person who cannot understand, override or stop the system is not oversight.

Transparency and Notification Duties (Article 50)

Situation Duty On
System interacts directly with people design it so people know they are dealing with AI, unless obvious provider
System generates synthetic audio, image, video or text mark outputs in a machine-readable format provider
Emotion recognition or biometric categorization inform the exposed people deployer
Deepfakes and AI text published to inform the public disclose it is artificial (editorial-control exceptions) deployer
  • Information is given clearly, at the latest at first interaction or exposure
  • Also: deployers of high-risk systems inform people subject to decisions (Article 26) and workers' representatives before workplace use
Exam tip

Telling a customer they are chatting with AI is the provider's design duty, unless it is obvious.

Quality Management System (Article 17)

  • A documented system of policies, procedures and instructions that keeps the provider compliant
  • Covers a compliance strategy, design and development controls, testing and validation, technical specifications, data management, risk management, post-market monitoring, serious incident reporting, communication with authorities, record-keeping, resource management and accountability
  • Applied proportionately to the provider's size, with consideration for SMEs
  • It is the provider's management layer over everything in Articles 9 to 15
Exam tip

The QMS ties the requirements into one managed system; it does not replace any of them.

5II.C.4: Explain what more the law asks of general-purpose AI models

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Understand, so the depth is Understand. The course has 1 practice question on this indicator.

General-Purpose AI Models: Obligations of All Providers [Dates]

  • Technical documentation of the model, including training and testing (Annex XI)
  • Information and documentation for downstream providers who build it into systems (Annex XII), protecting IP and trade secrets
  • A copyright policy that honors rights reservations
  • A public summary of training content using the AI Office template (Article 53)
  • These rules apply from 2 August 2025

Exam tip

These four duties apply to every general-purpose model; systemic-risk models add more.

Models With Systemic Risk (Articles 51 and 55) Beyond the BoK

  • A model has systemic risk if it has high-impact capabilities
  • It is presumed when training used more than 10^25 floating point operations, or the Commission so decides (Article 51)
  • Extra duties (Article 55): evaluate the model including adversarial testing; assess and mitigate systemic risks at EU level; track and report serious incidents to the AI Office; ensure cybersecurity
  • Helios: Corvid Labs, not Helios, carries the model-level duties; Helios, as a deployer, asks for the model documentation
Exam tip

The compute threshold gives a presumption, not the only route to systemic-risk status.

Codes of Practice, Open Source and the Provider Chain [Dates]

  • The AI Office encourages codes of practice covering the model duties; they were due by 2 May 2025
  • If a code is not finalized by 2 August 2025 or is inadequate, the Commission may set common rules by implementing act
  • Providers can show compliance through a code, harmonized standards, or other adequate means
  • Free and open-source models get relief from some duties, but not from the copyright policy and training summary, and not if they carry systemic risk
  • Downstream providers rely on the model provider's information to meet their own duties
Exam tip

A code of practice is a route to showing compliance, not a replacement for the duties.

6II.C.5: Explain how AI laws are enforced and what penalties apply

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Understand, so the depth is Understand. The course has 1 practice question on this indicator.

Governance and Who Enforces

  • European level: the AI Office (in the Commission) oversees general-purpose models; the AI Board helps coordinate
  • National level: each Member State designates at least one market surveillance authority and one notifying authority, acting independently
  • Notified bodies perform third-party conformity assessment where required
  • Market surveillance authorities can require corrective action, withdraw or recall systems and impose fines
  • The European Data Protection Supervisor supervises EU institutions

Exam tip

General-purpose model enforcement is European; most system enforcement is national.

Penalties

  • Prohibited practices (Article 5): up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher
  • Most other obligations (providers, importers, distributors, deployers, authorized representatives, notified bodies, transparency): up to EUR 15 million or 3%
  • Incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to authorities: up to EUR 7.5 million or 1%
  • SMEs and start-ups: the lower of the amount or the percentage
  • General-purpose model providers (Article 101): up to 3% or EUR 15 million, imposed by the Commission

Exam tip

Whichever is higher for large companies, whichever is lower for SMEs; do not confuse the GDPR's 20 million and 4%.

The Timeline [Dates] [Verify live]

  • 2 February 2025: prohibitions and the AI literacy duty
  • 2 August 2025: general-purpose model rules, governance and most penalties provisions
  • 2 August 2026: the Act applies generally, including transparency duties
  • 2 December 2026: the new bans on sexual imagery apply
  • 2 December 2027: Annex III high-risk rules; 2 August 2028: Annex I product-safety high-risk rules (as amended; earlier dates were sooner)
  • As of 27 October 2026: consolidated text dated 27 July 2026; check for further changes

Exam tip

Know the order: bans first, then general-purpose models, then general application, then high-risk.

7II.C.6: Explain how the duties differ by organizational role: provider, deployer, importer, distributor

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Understand, so the depth is Understand. The course has 1 practice question on this indicator.

Duties by Role: Providers, Importers, Distributors, Authorized Representatives

Role Main duties
Provider (Article 16) meet the requirements, quality management system, documentation and logs, conformity assessment, declaration, CE marking, registration, corrective action
Importer (Article 23) verify conformity, documentation, marking and instructions before placing on the market; keep key documents for 10 years; do not place non-conforming systems
Distributor check marking, documentation and instructions; stop if non-conforming; keep storage safe
Authorized representative (Article 22) acts for a non-EU provider under a written mandate
  • Each role has its own checks; none can rely on another's word alone
Exam tip

The importer and distributor are gatekeepers: they verify before they supply.

Deployer Duties and When a Role Changes

  • Use per instructions and assign human oversight to people with competence, training and authority (Article 26)
  • Ensure input data under your control are relevant and sufficiently representative
  • Monitor, tell the provider, suspend use where there is a risk, and report serious incidents (the provider first, then the authorities)
  • Keep logs for at least six months; inform workers' representatives and affected workers before workplace use, and inform people subject to decisions
  • A deployer becomes a provider if it puts its name on a high-risk system, makes a substantial modification, or changes the intended purpose so that it becomes high-risk (Article 25)
  • Helios: as deployer of the hiring tool, it must do all of the above

Exam tip

Rebranding or repurposing a high-risk system moves provider duties onto you.

8Other AI-specific laws named in the BoK

Exam angle

This is domain-level text, not an indicator, so no BoK verb sets its depth. The course asks no separate practice question on it; the laws appear in the questions on the indicators above.

South Korea: The AI Basic Act [Verify live]

  • In force from 22 January 2026 (secondary sources)
  • High-impact AI in areas such as healthcare, hiring and lending: risk management, user notice and human oversight duties
  • Generative AI: advance notice to users and labeling of generated output
  • Foreign operators above set thresholds appoint a domestic representative
  • Fines up to KRW 30 million, with a grace period of at least a year announced before fines
  • As of 27 October 2026: details rest on secondary reports; check the official text

Exam tip

Korea resembles the EU in risk focus and in generative-AI notice and labeling, with lighter penalties.

The US Federal Position [Verify live]

  • There is no comprehensive federal AI statute; agencies apply existing laws: the FTC on deception and unfairness, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) on employment, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) on credit, and others
  • Federal policy has moved toward removing barriers and uniform national rules
  • Executive Order 14365 (11 December 2025) directed a federal challenge to state AI laws; a Justice Department AI litigation task force was formalized on 9 January 2026
  • On 20 March 2026 the White House released non-binding recommendations for a national framework that would preempt state laws
  • As of 27 October 2026: no federal statute preempts state AI laws, so state and local laws still bind private companies
Exam tip

In the US, the answer to which law applies is usually existing federal law plus state and local AI-specific rules.

US State and Local AI Laws [Verify live]

  • Colorado: the 2024 AI Act was repealed and replaced by Senate Bill (SB) 26-189, signed 14 May 2026, effective 1 January 2027: consumer notice, explanations of adverse decisions, human review
  • Texas (House Bill, HB, 149): a narrow ban on intentionally harmful uses, with a notice-and-cure period and a sandbox
  • California: SB 53 frontier-model transparency and incident reporting (effective 1 January 2026); automated decision-making privacy rules
  • Illinois (HB 3773): employers notify employees of AI in employment decisions; no discriminatory use
  • New York City (Local Law 144): annual independent bias audit and candidate notice for hiring tools
  • As of 27 October 2026: these statuses rest on secondary reports; check each statute

Exam tip

For Helios's hiring in New York City and Illinois, the audit of an automated employment decision tool (AEDT) and the notice duty are the two to remember.

Other Jurisdictions: Approaches Compared Beyond the BoK [Verify live]

  • Risk-based statutes: the EU AI Act, South Korea, and Brazil's bill
  • Principles-based, regulator-led: the UK, with no general AI statute, and Japan's promotion-oriented law, leaning on cooperation and existing law
  • Technology-specific rules: China regulates algorithms, generative AI services and the labeling of AI-generated content
  • International instruments: the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI, the first binding AI treaty (opened 5 September 2024), and the OECD principles
  • As of 27 October 2026: these regimes are evolving, so the course teaches them as approaches

Exam tip

Questions on other jurisdictions ask for the approach, not article numbers.

Which Instrument Applies? A Decision Aid

  • Where is the system used and who is affected? That selects the jurisdictions
  • What does it do? That gives the class and the requirements
  • Who are you in the chain? That gives your duties
  • Which existing laws also apply (privacy, nondiscrimination, consumer protection, IP, liability) and which framework organizes the work (module 7)
  • Helios example: EU AI Act for the hiring tool and assistant; New York City and Illinois rules; GDPR; nondiscrimination law; Korea for its Korean customers

Exam tip

AI-specific laws sit on top of existing laws; they do not replace them.

9Exam Q&A

9.1 Practice questions (one best answer, or select exactly the number the question asks for)

S1Helios's hiring tool screens and ranks job applicants in the EU. How does the AI Act classify it?

  • AAs a prohibited practice, because all AI used in recruitment is banned in the Union under Article 5
  • BAs high-risk, because recruitment is an Annex III area and the tool profiles people
  • CAs limited risk, because the main duty is to tell applicants that they are interacting with AI
  • DAs minimal risk, because a recruiter makes the final decision about each applicant
Show the answer

Answer: B. Employment, including recruitment and selection, is an Annex III area, and a system that profiles natural persons cannot use the Article 6(3) exception. Recruitment AI is not banned, a human decision does not make it minimal, and transparency alone does not cover a high-risk use.

S2Which TWO practices are prohibited under Article 5 of the AI Act? (Select TWO.)

  • AInferring employees' emotions in the workplace, except for medical or safety reasons
  • BUsing a spam filter to sort a company's incoming email into folders and a junk folder
  • CScoring applicants for a bank loan with a model that estimates their creditworthiness
  • DBuilding a facial recognition database by untargeted scraping of internet or CCTV images
  • EShowing a notice that a customer is chatting with an AI system before the chat starts
Show the answer

Answer: A, D. Workplace emotion inference and untargeted facial scraping are banned. A spam filter is minimal risk, credit scoring is a high-risk use rather than a banned one, and a chatbot notice is a transparency duty that the Act requires.

S3A provider of a high-risk system must run a continuous, iterative process throughout the system's life cycle to identify and reduce foreseeable risks. Which requirement is this?

  • AThe data governance requirement in Article 10, which concerns the quality of training data
  • BThe human oversight requirement in Article 14, which concerns the people who monitor the system
  • CThe risk management system in Article 9, which runs throughout the life cycle of the system
  • DThe record-keeping requirement in Article 12, which concerns automatic logs of system events
Show the answer

Answer: C. Article 9 requires a risk management system that is a continuous iterative process planned and run throughout the entire life cycle. The other articles cover data, oversight and logs.

S4Helios's customer assistant chats directly with EU customers and is not used for any high-risk purpose. Which duty most directly applies?

  • ARegistering the assistant in the EU database of high-risk systems before it is used
  • BCarrying out a fundamental rights impact assessment before the first customer chat
  • CObtaining a conformity assessment from a notified body before offering the assistant
  • DMaking sure customers are informed that they are interacting with an AI system
Show the answer

Answer: D. A system that interacts directly with people carries a transparency duty under Article 50: people must be told they are dealing with AI, unless it is obvious. Registration, a notified-body assessment and a fundamental rights impact assessment belong to high-risk systems.

S5Corvid Labs trains a general-purpose model using more than 10^25 floating point operations. What follows under the AI Act?

  • AThe model is exempt from the Act, because the Act regulates AI systems and not models
  • BThe model is presumed to have systemic risk, so its provider takes on extra duties
  • CThe model must be withdrawn from the EU market until a notified body has certified it for use
  • DThe model becomes a prohibited practice, because training at that scale is banned in the Union
Show the answer

Answer: B. Training above that compute threshold creates a presumption of high-impact capabilities and so of systemic risk, which adds duties such as model evaluation with adversarial testing, risk mitigation, incident reporting and cybersecurity. Models are regulated, and scale alone does not prohibit or require certification.

S6What is the maximum fine for using a prohibited AI practice under the AI Act?

  • AEUR 7.5 million or 1% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher
  • BEUR 15 million or 3% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher
  • CEUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher
  • DEUR 20 million or 4% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher
Show the answer

Answer: C. Prohibited practices carry the top tier: up to EUR 35 million or 7%, whichever is higher. The lower tiers cover other obligations and incorrect information, and the EUR 20 million and 4% tier belongs to the GDPR.

S7Helios deploys the Veridex hiring tool, which is a high-risk system. Which TWO duties fall on Helios as the deployer? (Select TWO.)

  • ADrawing up the EU declaration of conformity and affixing the CE marking to the tool itself
  • BUsing the tool as instructed and assigning competent, trained people to oversee it
  • CRunning the quality management system that covers the tool's design and development work
  • DRegistering the tool as the provider and keeping its technical documentation up to date
  • EInforming workers' representatives and affected people that the tool is in use
Show the answer

Answer: B, E. Deployers use the system as instructed, assign competent oversight, and inform workers' representatives and the affected people. The declaration, CE marking, quality management system, registration as provider and technical documentation are provider duties.

10Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Classes prohibited, high-risk (Annex I and Annex III), transparency, minimal; general-purpose models on their own track
High-risk Articles 9 to 15 requirements, conformity assessment, registration, FRIA, post-market monitoring, incident reports (15, 10 and 2 days)
Oversight, transparency, QMS effective human oversight; tell people they deal with AI; a documented quality system
GPAI four duties for all; systemic-risk models add evaluations, risk mitigation, incident reporting and cybersecurity
Penalties EUR 35 million or 7%; EUR 15 million or 3%; EUR 7.5 million or 1%; roles carry different duties
Beyond the EU Korea, US federal and state laws, and other approaches

module.title: AI-Specific Laws: the EU AI Act and Beyond
